newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ex-finmin Madelin urges lower French, German rates.
newsitem.headline: Ex-finmin Madelin urges lower French, German rates.

text.p: Former French Finance Minister Alain Madelin said on Sunday that France and Germany should ease interest rates.

Madelin, a fervent free-marketeer deputy in the UDF party, told TF1 television the pressure on the German mark and French franc resulting from easier monetary policies would not be a bad thing as they are overvalued against the U.S. dollar.
He said he did not believe the franc and mark should be uncoupled, as former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing recently proposed in Parliament, sparking a debate on the currency.
"But maybe Giscard's proposals will help to reinforce the dialogue -- we need to make the Germans understand the need now to manage our monetary policies jointly," Madelin said.

"It would be in the interests of France and Germany to ease credit. That would lead to a small depreciation in the franc and mark against the dollar, but that wouldn't be a bad thing as these currencies are overvalued today against the dollar," he said.
Madelin said, "If the euro (single currency) were chronically overvalued against the dollar, with higher interest rates, it would be dangerous for Europe."
French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl reaffirmed on Saturday their commitment to a stable franc-mark rate in the run-up to a single European currency.

Their comments after talks in the southwestern French town of Perigueux followed 10 days of fierce debate over Giscard d'Estaing's call for a depreciation of the franc to revive economic growth and combat record unemployment.
